story.title: Saudi Arabia Suspends Flights After Houthi Attacks on Riyadh Airport
story.summary: Saudi Arabia has suspended all flights to and from King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh following a series of missile attacks by the Houthi rebel group. The attacks, which occurred on October 10 and 11, resulted in at least 13 fatalities and numerous injuries. The situation has prompted discussions about potential U.S. involvement in the conflict as regional allies call for stronger defense measures.

timeline_highlights.title: Trump Issues Threats Against Iranian Infrastructure Amid Strait of Hormuz Tensions
timeline_highlights.summary: US President Donald Trump has threatened to target Iranian bridges and power plants in retaliation for any attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz. He stated that for each ship fired upon by Iranian forces, the US would respond by destroying a corresponding piece of Iranian infrastructure. This escalation comes amid ongoing tensions in the region and rising oil prices.

The threat follows continued Iranian attacks on shipping in the region.
Oil prices have surged amid the escalating tensions.

The attack occurred on October 8 and is reported to be the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom launched a major military offensive against the Houthis the previous weekend. timeline_highlights.title: Deadly Houthi Attacks on Riyadh Airport Leave 12 Dead and Hundreds Injured
timeline_highlights.summary: A series of attacks attributed to the Iran-backed Houthi militia targeted Riyadh's international airport, resulting in at least 12 fatalities and over 300 injuries. The Saudi-led coalition has condemned the strikes as a 'war crime' and vowed a decisive response. Following the initial attack, a second projectile struck the airport, causing further damage and prompting the closure of the facility and the transition of local schools to online learning.
key_facts: At least 12 people killed and over 300 injured in attacks on Riyadh airport.
The attacks were attributed to the Iran-backed Houthi militia.
A second projectile struck the airport a day after the initial attack.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War is the 2026 armed conflict that began with U.S. and Israeli military strikes on Iran on February 28, followed by Iranian retaliatory attacks and a widening regional security crisis. It has included fighting affecting Iran and neighboring Gulf states, as well as repeated threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz; diplomatic contacts and temporary arrangements have not resolved the underlying conflict.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: The current phase of the conflict began on February 28, 2026. The International Maritime Organization described the Strait of Hormuz crisis as unresolved on August 28, six months after the conflict began.

facts.label: Main parties and geography
facts.value: The conflict centers on military action by the United States and Israel against Iran and Iranian retaliatory activity across the region. Its regional effects have included attacks or alleged attacks involving Gulf states and risks to shipping in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, and Strait of Hormuz.

facts.label: U.S. military operation
facts.value: U.S. Central Command calls its campaign against Iran Operation Epic Fury. The U.S. government has said the operation was directed at Iranian military and security targets and was intended, among other stated purposes, to protect U.S. forces and maritime commerce through the Strait of Hormuz.

facts.label: Strait of Hormuz significance
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a major international shipping passage whose traffic-separation scheme was proposed by Iran and Oman and adopted by the International Maritime Organization in 1968. The IMO says attacks, disruptions, and safety risks in the strait have left seafarers and vessels exposed during the conflict.

facts.label: International response
facts.value: The United Nations Security Council addressed the escalation on February 28, 2026, and the UN Secretary-General called for de-escalation, dialogue, and adherence to international law and international humanitarian law. The IMO has separately urged states and maritime actors to protect civilian seafarers and restore safe navigation.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on late-July 2026 escalation, U.S. war-powers debate, Houthi-linked developments, and ceasefire-related diplomacy; it does not attempt to cover the full military, humanitarian, legal, or diplomatic record of the conflict.

explore_lenses.label: What changed at Riyadh airport after the attacks?
explore_lenses.title: Closure extended amid renewed strike risk
explore_lenses.summary: The disruption moved beyond flight diversions after the October 10 strike: Saudi authorities kept King Khalid International Airport closed while conducting safety checks and responding to further reported missile and drone threats.

claims.text: Reporting on October 12 said Saudi authorities extended the suspension of all flights at King Khalid International Airport after a further attack, citing the need to verify the airport's safety.

The airport disruption had already led airlines to cancel or divert flights; Kuwait Airways specifically cited the airport closure and security situation when cancelling Riyadh services on October 10.

The casualty total is still evolving across reports: one October 12 account put the October 10 death toll at 13 and said a later strike killed one more person, while another reported 14 deaths over the weekend.

explore_lenses.label: How did the airport become a Houthi target?
explore_lenses.title: A Yemen counteroffensive widened the conflict
explore_lenses.summary: The attacks are reported in the context of a renewed Yemen war: Saudi-backed government forces began a counteroffensive against Houthi-held strategic terrain, while the Houthis portray attacks on Saudi targets as reciprocal to Saudi military action.

claims.text: The Guardian reported that Yemeni government forces and local allies began a counteroffensive aimed at driving Houthi forces from the Bab al-Mandab area and other positions; Saudi support for the UN-backed Yemeni government is presented as a central reason the kingdom is being targeted.

Houthi statements carried by Al-Masirah said their actions were guided by reciprocity and warned that more attacks would follow unless Saudi Arabia stopped its military action and involvement in Yemen.

Saudi officials are framing the immediate priority as resilience and defence: the energy minister said the kingdom would confront the crisis, while the military reported additional missile and drone threats.
A security analyst cited by the Guardian said Saudi air defences can intercept some attacks but cannot reliably protect a country of Saudi Arabia's size at all times.

Houthi statements carried by Al-Masirah said their actions were guided by reciprocity and warned that more attacks would follow unless Saudi Arabia stopped its military action and involvement in Yemen.

Saudi officials are framing the immediate priority as resilience and defence: the energy minister said the kingdom would confront the crisis, while the military reported additional missile and drone threats.
A security analyst cited by the Guardian said Saudi air defences can intercept some attacks but cannot reliably protect a country of Saudi Arabia's size at all times.

story_report.summary: Saudi Arabia has halted flights to and from King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh after Houthi missile attacks struck the airport. The attacks on October 10 and 11 killed at least 13 people and injured hundreds, according to the reviewed reporting. Authorities later extended the shutdown after a further attack while safety checks were carried out, with flights announced as suspended until next Saturday. The disruption has prompted cancellations and diversions, while Gulf partners press for stronger defensive coordination.

sections.heading: Airport Closure Disrupts Regional Aviation
sections.body: The closure had already forced airlines to cancel or divert services. Kuwait Airways cancelled Riyadh flights on October 10, citing both the airport closure and the security situation. Saudi authorities said the extended suspension was needed to verify that the airport was safe after the further attack, making the immediate aviation disruption dependent on security assessments rather than a confirmed restoration timetable.

sections.heading: Yemen Conflict Drives Riyadh Attacks
sections.body: The Guardian reported that Yemeni government forces and local allies had begun a counteroffensive against Houthi positions around Bab al-Mandab and elsewhere. It described Saudi support for Yemen's UN-backed government as a central reason the kingdom is being targeted. In statements carried by Al-Masirah, the Houthis portrayed their attacks as reciprocal and said they would continue unless Saudi Arabia stopped its military action and involvement in Yemen; Saudi officials, meanwhile, emphasized resilience and air defence.

sections.heading: Gulf States Seek Defence Coordination
sections.body: A UAE official called for stronger Gulf security and defence cooperation, signaling a push for coordinated protection rather than a publicly announced joint offensive. Iran's foreign minister spoke with his Saudi counterpart on October 11 about whether Tehran could mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. The Guardian also reported that the UN Security Council was expected to meet on October 13 over a proposed resolution designating the Houthis a foreign terrorist organization.
